title: Beyond the Leaderboard: Building a Codex-Powered Improvement Harness on ViralBench
subtitle: A proposed workflow for improving ViralBench agents: inspect their decisions, replay the task, and independently evaluate changes before release.
author: Sulayman Bowles
seoTitle: ViralBench + Codex: Building an AI Agent Evaluation Harness
seoDescription: A proposed workflow for improving ViralBench agents: inspect their decisions, replay the task, and independently evaluate changes before release.
excerpt: ViralBench puts AI agents inside a live attention market. This design proposes a Codex engineering layer that inspects failed runs, tests changes through replay, and submits candidates for independent evaluation before release.
markdown:
*ViralBench asks AI agents to earn views on TikTok. I am designing an improvement harness around it: Codex would inspect failed runs, propose patches, and test them against retained evidence. Independent evaluation and deployment approval would stay outside its control.*

Most AI benchmarks stop when the model returns an answer.

[ViralBench](https://viralbench.ai/) gives frontier models real TikTok accounts, current social-content research, reference-post inspection, image generation, slideshow rendering, and publishing tools. They pursue views in the fitness category, inspect account performance, and try again.

The agent must research, interpret images, choose a thesis, allocate its tool budget, create and inspect a post, publish, and learn from delayed feedback. A static prompt set tests fewer of these decisions; fluency alone cannot establish success.

The methodology and code audit expose the working loop: research, image generation, review, publishing, and account feedback.

I would build an experimental harness around this open-source loop, with Codex as its engineering agent.

Codex would improve the system that makes the carousel. It would inspect traces, form a narrow hypothesis, edit a defined repository surface, run replay tests, and submit a reviewable patch for a controlled live trial.

The proposed division of work:

> The ViralBench agent makes the post. Codex proposes improvements to the agent.

## ViralBench is a live agent environment

The public experiment compares GPT-5.5, Claude Opus 4.8, and Kimi. Each receives two warmed-up TikTok accounts and runs around 7 AM and 5 PM Central Time, pursuing views in the fitness category.[^1]

I reviewed the standalone handoff: one 937-line TypeScript file containing the prompt, agent loop, API clients, media handling, account telemetry, memory, rendering, publishing, and run persistence.[^2] Unlike the two-account live competition, it uses one account and leaves a reviewable draft by default rather than scheduling publication.

The agent has up to 18 rounds and five tools:

| Capability | Implementation in the current agent | What the model is deciding |
|---|---|---|
| Current-content research | `call_lightreel_api` | Which trends, hooks, scripts, and formats are worth investigating |
| Visual inspection | `view_media` through ScrapeCreators | Which reference posts to study and which slides matter |
| Asset creation | `generate_image` through Doublespeed | What each slide should depict and which reference image to carry forward |
| Self-review | `preview_slideshow` | Whether the composed carousel is readable, coherent, and visually convincing |
| Publishing | `publish_slideshow` through Doublespeed | Which account receives the post, with what caption and optional sound |

TikTok and Instagram URLs resolve to images, which are resized, labeled, and returned to the vision-capable model. Generated images also receive labels and can guide later generations, giving the model visual working memory within a run.

Each run allows six Lightreel research calls, at most one per round, up to 12 viewed reference images per round, and 18 working rounds. OpenRouter calls the main model with an append-only conversation history. Same-round actions execute concurrently.

The workflow:

```text
Account performance and prior notes
                ↓
Current-culture research
                ↓
Full-post visual inspection
                ↓
Content thesis and slide design
                ↓
Image generation and image-to-image adaptation
                ↓
Rendered slideshow preview
                ↓
Revision
                ↓
Draft or scheduled post
                ↓
Delayed TikTok metrics
```

The model cannot know whether retrieved examples are representative or observe TikTok’s distribution mechanism. Feedback comes from few posts: a strong post may receive weak distribution, while a mediocre one catches a passing wave. The agent must decide whether to repeat, alter, or abandon each format.

ViralBench tests decisions under partial observability, limited actions, changing conditions, and delayed rewards.

## What the current code gets right

The prompt requires external research rather than relying on training data for current culture. A limited budget makes the agent choose its questions.

The model can inspect source carousels, generated images, and the final text-on-image composition. It can judge visible artifacts rather than describe what a text-only critic imagines.

One file exposes the control flow, tools, limits, failure handling, and memory. That makes the handoff easy to inspect.

Views are imperfect evidence, but the response comes from the platform.

The public handoff stops at a draft, preserving human review even though the live benchmark can publish autonomously. I would retain that boundary for company or client accounts.

The code contains the inner loop. Infrastructure for testing improvement remains to be built.

## The leaderboard is a system result, not a pure model score

ViralBench measures an assembled marketing system. Its leaderboard needs to be read accordingly.

A post’s result depends on:

```text
result = f(
  language model,
  system prompt,
  tool definitions,
  retrieval quality,
  reference-content selection,
  image model,
  account history,
  memory,
  posting time,
  publishing infrastructure,
  current TikTok conditions,
  random distribution effects
)
```

The result can change with the base model, Lightreel query, image generator, copying instructions, account history, sound, or posting time.

The leaderboard is a **live system benchmark**, or **field trial of agent stacks**. It cannot isolate model intelligence.

That is commercially relevant: companies deploy models with prompts, tools, data, permissions, interfaces, and controls. They need the assembled system to work.

A weekly winner may have used the harness better, found a format suited to its account, imitated a successful post, or received favorable distribution. Winning alone cannot establish superior marketing reasoning.

I would analyze each **model-plus-harness configuration**, not the model name alone.

Tie each result to a versioned configuration, state each change’s hypothesis, and distinguish estimated lift from lucky outliers before promotion.

## What the code audit reveals

The file’s header describes a self-contained handoff, not an experimentation platform. Its gaps define the engineering work ahead.

### 1. The run record is too thin to explain success or failure

The local `.marketing-agent-runs.json` records the goal, published posts, final answer, reflection note, and round count.

It does not preserve the complete message history, individual tool inputs and outputs, Lightreel source material, viewed-media lineage, image prompts, preview assets, model usage, latency, cost, configuration hash, Git commit, or account-metric snapshots.

A winning post may leave no explanation. A failed run may leave no trace that distinguishes retrieval, generation, publishing, and model errors.

The trace must become the improvement harness’s primary dataset.

### 2. Several important constraints exist only as prompt prose

The prompt requires previewing before publication, a distinct image per slide, exactly one post per account, and completion before the final answer.

The runtime enforces maximum posts per account but accepts a final answer without checking the minimum. It requires no successful preview token, rejects no duplicate image URLs, and does not validate slide count, copy length, text fit, unsupported claims, or generation lineage.

Prompts influence behavior. Code must enforce these invariants.

### 3. Visual review is incomplete for longer carousels

Preview renders at most six slides. A longer carousel can reach publication with its final slides unseen.

Render every slide or block publication.

### 4. Cross-run memory is compressed into free-form notes

Future runs load up to ten model-written reflection notes as their only durable strategic memory.

These notes mix facts, interpretations, and narrative without checking them against the trace. They provide no stable representation of tested hypotheses, confidence, failed formats, account-specific effects, or unresolved questions.

The model writes its memory without an evidence check.

### 5. Account telemetry has attribution edge cases

The code refreshes recent posts’ TikTok metrics through ScrapeCreators when a public URL exists. Without one, it matches a profile post using a normalized caption prefix.

Similar captions can produce false matches. An experiment ledger needs stable post IDs and metric provenance.

### 6. Same-round parallelism creates hidden execution semantics

`Promise.all` runs same-round actions concurrently. This suits independent actions, but one image generation cannot reliably use another’s new label in that round. It must wait until a later round.

The prompt leaves this dependency implicit. A typed planner or action graph would express it.

### 7. The content-acquisition strategy creates provenance risk

The prompt asks the agent to adapt successful posts’ language closely and sometimes mirror their slide sequence. That may help short-term results, but it conflates:

- learning a general format;
- adapting a common hook pattern;
- paraphrasing a specific creator’s copy;
- reproducing a distinctive sequence or visual treatment.

The code neither retains a source graph nor measures reference-to-artifact similarity.

The agent should learn why a post works without reproducing a creator’s distinctive work.

### 8. The package is not fully reproducible as shipped

The source imports `sharp` for resizing and instructs users to install it, but `package.json` omits the dependency.

Unattended tests need a clean installation. The manifest must declare what the code imports.

These gaps separate a working agent from a system capable of causal evaluation, regression testing, controlled autonomy, and reproducible engineering.

## What I mean by “Codex as a harness”

OpenAI describes the Codex harness as the loop and execution logic connecting a model to instructions, tools, filesystem operations, and feedback.[^3] Its harness-engineering work also includes the repository, documentation, tests, review process, execution environment, and validation rules that govern reliable work.[^4]

In this design, ViralBench is the executable marketing environment. Codex works on it from outside the content-production loop.

I would assign these roles:

| Possible role | Decision |
|---|---|
| Generate the actual TikTok content | Not the primary role; the inner marketing agent already does this |
| Modify the marketing agent’s code, prompts, tools, and tests | Yes |
| Interpret traces and propose experiments | Yes, within an evidence-bound task |
| Decide whether its own change is successful and deploy it to production | No |

An agent that could change the evaluator, run a treatment, redefine success, and deploy its patch could game the metric or erode policy. Codex must not control that sequence.

I would separate five functions:

1. **The inner agent** researches, creates, previews, and submits a post.
2. **The recorder** captures raw evidence, actions, artifacts, and outcomes.
3. **The evaluator** applies versioned checks and statistical rules.
4. **Codex** diagnoses a bounded issue and produces a patch in an isolated worktree.
5. **The release controller** decides whether the candidate can enter replay, draft canary, or live deployment.

The proposed control flow:

```text
                  LIVE ENVIRONMENT
      Lightreel / TikTok / Doublespeed / media APIs
                         ↑       ↓
                ┌───────────────────┐
                │ ViralBench agent  │
                │   inner loop      │
                └───────────────────┘
                         ↓
          immutable traces, sources, artifacts,
            configuration, cost, metric snapshots
                         ↓
                ┌───────────────────┐
                │ Evaluation layer  │
                │ checks + analysis │
                └───────────────────┘
                         ↓
              bounded experiment candidate
                         ↓
                ┌───────────────────┐
                │ Codex worktree    │
                │ plan / patch/test │
                └───────────────────┘
                         ↓
             offline replay and regression gate
                         ↓
               human-approved draft canary
                         ↓
                 locked online evaluator
                         ↓
                   promote or revert
```

This would be a controlled software-improvement loop, with Codex doing the engineering under independent checks.

## The evidence layer comes before the Codex layer

Atlas taught me to separate raw observations from derived judgments.

An HTTP response, rendered DOM, sitemap entry, schema block, or search result is evidence. An issue label, score, or recommendation interprets it. Interpretations can change; observations must remain inspectable.

For ViralBench, each run should preserve an immutable evidence bundle:

- the Git commit and experiment manifest;
- model provider, model version, reasoning settings, and sampling parameters;
- the exact system prompt and tool schemas;
- account state at the beginning of the run;
- every Lightreel query and response;
- every source URL and retrieved media item;
- hashes of source and generated images;
- image prompts and reference-image lineage;
- every preview render;
- the final slide data and caption;
- publishing response and stable TikTok post ID;
- token usage, API cost, latency, and tool errors;
- metrics captured at fixed post-publication windows;
- human review decisions and reasons.

Store derived judgments separately:

- “insufficient research breadth”;
- “slide 1 text is likely unreadable”;
- “final copy is too similar to source post X”;
- “the treatment improved account-normalized 72-hour views”;
- “the agent repeated a failed format despite contrary evidence.”

Each finding should cite its supporting evidence IDs. Codex may propose findings and patches; it must not rewrite the raw trace.

These records make failures reproducible, supply training data for evaluators, and give Codex material to investigate. They also let reviewers check model-written explanations against events.

## The experiment is the unit of change

“Make the agent more viral” is too broad to test. Codex needs a falsifiable hypothesis and protected variables.

An example:

```yaml
experiment_id: visual-critic-v1
hypothesis: >
  A separate visual-critique pass after rendering will reduce
  text-overflow, repeated-image, and synthetic-looking-image failures
  without lowering 72-hour account-normalized views.

baseline_commit: 5f5f57e251023ceb37961c0fc2c808f67ceb71eb
editable_surfaces:
  - agent/critics/visual.ts
  - evals/visual/*
  - experiments/visual-critic-v1.yaml

protected_surfaces:
  - evals/online/primary-metric.ts
  - policies/publish-gateway.ts
  - traces/raw/*
  - secrets/*

offline_gates:
  - all_slides_rendered
  - no_duplicate_images
  - no_text_overflow
  - source_lineage_complete
  - historical_replay_pass_rate >= 0.95

live_design:
  unit: post
  blocking:
    - account
    - posting_slot
    - calendar_week
  primary_window: 72h
  minimum_pairs: 20

primary_metric: account_adjusted_log_views_72h
guardrails:
  - publish_failure_rate <= baseline
  - median_cost_per_post <= baseline * 1.15
  - policy_violation_count == 0
  - source_similarity_high_risk_count == 0

promotion_rule: >
  Pass every hard guardrail and show a positive primary-metric estimate
  with the pre-registered uncertainty threshold.
```

Define the hypothesis, editable scope, validation commands, metrics, guardrails, and stopping rule before Codex edits code or anyone sees live results.

A rejected experiment still records what failed. A defined contract makes both acceptance and rejection reviewable.

## Offline replay should absorb most iteration

Live trials take time, produce noisy results, and consume accounts, posting slots, API spend, and attention. Parser and prompt changes should first face replay.

Convert historical calls into versioned fixtures:

- frozen Lightreel responses;
- saved TikTok and Instagram media metadata;
- locally stored reference images or content-addressed snapshots;
- Doublespeed style presets and render responses;
- account-statistics snapshots;
- image-generation stubs or a fixed asset bank;
- publishing mocks;
- known failure responses from each dependency.

Run the inner agent repeatedly against the same recorded state to compare prompts, tool schemas, memory, and model substitutions.

Replay cannot predict views. It can test whether a post is ready for a live trial.

### Deterministic checks

Check these failures without another model:

- Did the agent remain within its research and round budgets?
- Did it inspect source material before generating?
- Was every generated asset linked to a valid reference or explicit text-only path?
- Was every slide rendered?
- Were duplicate image URLs rejected?
- Did publication occur only after a passing preview?
- Did the final account count match the experiment contract?
- Were claims, source IDs, and artifact hashes complete?
- Did the agent recover correctly from a tool timeout?
- Did it leave the repository and fixture state clean?

### Rubric-based checks

Other qualities need judgment:

- Is the first slide visually legible at mobile size?
- Does the carousel maintain a coherent subject across slides?
- Does the copy preserve the mechanism of a reference without reproducing it?
- Does the post contain unsupported fitness or health claims?
- Does the final creative look internally consistent?

Give model-based graders the evidence and a narrow rubric. Their scores remain judgments, not ground truth.

### Adversarial and fault-injection cases

Inject dependency failures:

- Lightreel returns a plausible but source-poor answer.
- ScrapeCreators resolves only half of a carousel.
- A reference image is too large or corrupt.
- Image generation returns the same asset twice.
- The renderer clips the last line of text.
- Sound extraction fails.
- Doublespeed creates a draft but returns no public review URL.
- TikTok metrics arrive late.
- Two profile posts have nearly identical caption prefixes.
- The model attempts to finish before publishing the required artifact.

The agent should stop safely and retain a diagnostic trace.

OpenAI’s evaluation guidance combines prompts, captured runs, traces, artifacts, checks, and comparable scores.[^5] I would use that structure here.

## Live evaluation needs experimental discipline

After passing replay, a candidate could enter a controlled live trial. Poor measurement here can turn market noise into apparent progress.

### Views are noisy and path-dependent

Account history, content supply, audience, timing, trend decay, sound, source similarity, and platform distribution all affect TikTok outcomes. The same creative cannot reach the same audience twice under identical conditions.

Successful posts also change an account’s audience and later distribution. The experiment is sequential; its observations are not independent static rows.

Raw mean views can mislead with small samples and rare winners. Online business metrics often have skewed, heavy-tailed distributions; controlled experiments use robust estimators, covariate adjustment, and longitudinal methods to address them.[^6]

### The trial should be blocked and paired

With few accounts and slots, I would block trials rather than compare treatment posts with historical controls.

Pair each candidate with a concurrent baseline, controlling where possible for:

- account;
- morning or evening slot;
- day or calendar week;
- broad content lane;
- recent account performance;
- number of slides;
- use of sound;
- paid or organic distribution, if that ever changes.

A switchback or crossover could alternate baseline and treatment across comparable account-slot blocks. Pre-experiment performance could serve as a covariate, using variance-reduction methods such as CUPED to account for different starting levels.[^7]

### Measurement windows should be fixed in advance

Capture views and engagement at fixed horizons, such as:

- one hour;
- six hours;
- 24 hours;
- 72 hours;
- seven days.

Choose the primary horizon before the trial. A favorable six-hour result cannot replace a planned 72-hour result.

I would analyze an account-adjusted `log(1 + views)` alongside the raw distribution. The log scale limits an extreme post’s influence; median and trimmed-mean comparisons would check robustness.

Display every raw result. Robust analysis limits outliers’ influence without hiding them.

### Hard guardrails should precede optimization

Hard constraints should stand outside a weighted score. Views cannot compensate for copyright risk, misleading health claims, or missing disclosure.

The proposed objective:

```text
maximize expected account-adjusted views at the locked horizon

subject to:
- platform and disclosure requirements pass
- source-provenance checks pass
- factual and health-claim checks pass
- publishing and rollback checks pass
- cost remains within budget
- human approval is present where required
```

Only candidates that pass these constraints compete on views.

### A/B tests and bandits answer different questions

A multi-armed bandit could allocate posts to promising strategies. It cannot replace causal evaluation.

An A/B or switchback trial asks whether a change improved outcomes under comparable conditions.

A bandit chooses where to allocate the next unit of traffic or publishing capacity, balancing reward and learning.

I would validate harness changes with controlled trials, then use bounded bandits to allocate among proven strategies. Prematurely mixing inference and allocation can obscure why views increased.

## Codex should receive bounded engineering tasks

Codex can inspect, edit, and run code through its CLI, non-interactive `codex exec`, TypeScript SDK, or an orchestration layer.[^8] The SDK can start and resume coding threads programmatically. Worktrees isolate experiments; sandbox policies restrict writes.[^9]

I would begin with `codex exec` in CI and a structured output schema. The SDK could later support persistent experiment threads and staged tasks.

Each task should define:

- a single concrete goal;
- the working directory and base commit;
- task mode;
- files that may be edited;
- protected paths;
- raw evidence inputs;
- known failure reproduction;
- required tests and replay suites;
- artifact locations;
- output schema;
- done criteria;
- conditions that require stopping rather than guessing.

I plan to support these task modes:

| Mode | Codex may do | Required output |
|---|---|---|
| Plan | Inspect evidence and propose an implementation | `EXEC_PLAN.md`, affected files, risks, test plan |
| Review | Inspect a patch or run without changing code | Findings tied to file lines and trace IDs |
| Implement | Modify a bounded surface | Patch, tests, results, migration notes |
| Debug | Reproduce a known failure and fix its cause | Reproduction, root cause, regression test, patch |
| Benchmark / Eval | Add or run evaluation cases | Versioned dataset, grader/check, comparative report |
| Visual QA | Inspect rendered artifacts and visual checks | Scored report with artifact references |
| Deploy | Promote an already-approved candidate | Release record, checksums, rollback pointer |

“Deploy” would execute an approved release, with no authority to approve it.

An illustrative handoff:

```text
Mode: Implement
Goal: Make a successful full-slideshow preview a hard prerequisite for publishing.

Evidence:
- Trace VB-2026-07-08-017 published eight slides after previewing only six.
- The current preview function caps max_slides at six.
- publish_slideshow has no preview receipt check.

Editable paths:
- agent/rendering/**
- agent/publishing/**
- evals/preview-gate/**

Do not edit:
- evals/online/**
- policies/**
- traces/raw/**
- experiment promotion thresholds

Verification:
- npm test
- npm run eval:preview-gate
- npm run replay -- --case VB-2026-07-08-017

Done when:
- every slide is rendered or publication is blocked;
- a preview receipt is bound to the exact slide payload;
- the historical failure becomes a passing regression case;
- RESULTS.md contains commands, results, changed files, and remaining risks.
```

This task specifies behavior a human can review. “Improve visual quality” leaves success undefined.

## The repository itself must become legible to Codex

Codex needs relevant knowledge in its repository. OpenAI’s harness-engineering work emphasizes that information confined to chats, external documents, or memory is unavailable to the agent while it works.[^4]

I would split the handoff into modules and versioned artifacts:

```text
/agent
  /policy              system prompts, action schemas, run policy
  /runtime             loop, state machine, dependency handling
  /memory              structured cross-run state

/tools
  /lightreel
  /media
  /images
  /rendering
  /publishing
  /metrics

/experiments
  /manifests            hypotheses, protected variables, promotion rules
  /candidates           Codex-ready tasks and results

/replay
  /fixtures             frozen external responses and assets
  /worlds               named historical environment states
  /faults               dependency and data failure scenarios

/evals
  /deterministic
  /rubrics
  /visual
  /online
  /regression

/traces
  /raw                  append-only event records
  /indexes              searchable run and artifact indexes

/artifacts
  /source-media
  /generated-media
  /previews
  /published

/reports
  /runs
  /experiments
  /leaderboard

/codex
  AGENTS.md
  /skills
  /schemas
  /hooks
  /task-templates

/policies
  publish-gateway.ts
  provenance.ts
  platform-compliance.ts
  health-claims.ts
  cost-limits.ts
```

`AGENTS.md` should point to architecture, evidence contracts, task modes, checks, and protected paths. Detailed decisions belong beside the code they govern, in versioned documents and schemas.

Hooks could require an experiment ID, protect restricted files, validate result-to-trace references, and confirm required evaluations before accepting a pull request. Code would enforce the task contract.

## Memory should become structured belief, not autobiography

The existing reflection note could remain, but structured memory should separate:

- observation;
- hypothesis;
- decision;
- result;
- confidence;
- scope;
- expiration.

An example:

```json
{
  "belief_id": "BEL-0041",
  "account": "fitness-account-a",
  "claim": "Beginner mistake carousels outperform motivation quotes in the evening slot",
  "evidence_runs": ["RUN-0108", "RUN-0112", "RUN-0117"],
  "counterevidence_runs": ["RUN-0120"],
  "confidence": 0.63,
  "valid_from": "2026-07-01",
  "review_after": "2026-07-15",
  "status": "provisional"
}
```

The system could propose structured beliefs from traces while still allowing narrative notes. Evidence links must be valid.

Expire or discount beliefs when their evidence ages, the account changes, or results contradict them.

Keep a small, contestable set of beliefs. Repetition must not become evidence.

## Provenance is a product requirement, not an afterthought

Because the current agent closely adapts winning content, I would add provenance early.

Record each final slide’s lineage:

```text
final slide
  ├── generated image hash
  │     ├── generation prompt
  │     ├── image model and version
  │     └── reference source image hash
  ├── overlay text
  │     ├── source post(s) consulted
  │     ├── similarity score
  │     └── transformation rationale
  └── visual structure
        ├── source pattern tags
        └── originality / duplication checks
```

“Problem, explanation, correction, payoff” is a common pattern. A creator’s distinctive sentences, examples, and compositions may be reproduction. The evaluator should flag that distinction for review.

Provenance should include AI disclosure. TikTok requires labels for realistic AI-generated images, audio, and video, and may apply labels through Content Credentials.[^10] ViralBench prompts seek realistic, native-looking imagery. The publishing harness should retain disclosure metadata and block publication if it cannot verify a required setting.

A views-only objective may reward extreme nutrition claims, impossible transformations, or fear-based advice. Claims about health, injury, supplementation, or disease should pass a separate evidence and policy check before publication.

## “Maximize views” is a useful benchmark objective and an incomplete business objective

The current goal makes views the sole objective, excluding brand safety, selling, and follower count.

That gives the agent a measurable target rather than a marketing answer it can describe but never test.

It may also favor copied hooks, outrage, exaggerated promises, high-arousal content, or account tactics that sacrifice future performance.

I would separate two modes.

### Benchmark mode

Study attention capture under controlled conditions.

Optimize account-adjusted views subject to platform policy, disclosure, provenance, factuality, cost, and publishing constraints.

### Enterprise mode

Measure business outcomes:

- qualified reach;
- attributable site visits;
- assisted conversions;
- customer acquisition cost;
- lead quality;
- retention or repeat engagement;
- brand and compliance constraints.

These metrics differ in horizon and causal role. A weighted score cannot resolve those differences; the harness should separate leading indicators from outcomes and record attribution uncertainty.

Broad reach may yield no commercial value; a few views from the right audience may matter greatly.

ViralBench’s visible reward makes it a useful laboratory. A commercial system needs downstream evidence and constraints before it can connect views to revenue.

## The first build sequence

First make the baseline reproducible and observable. Prompt changes can wait.

### Phase 0: Freeze and document the baseline

- Pin the current commit and dependency versions.
- Add the missing `sharp` dependency and a lockfile.
- Record the exact live and handoff configurations separately.
- Create an architecture map and a canonical run schema.
- Save a small set of representative historical runs as reference cases.

Deliverable: an installable, replayable baseline.

### Phase 1: Add complete traces and hard runtime invariants

- Replace the thin snapshot with append-only event traces.
- Hash prompts, tool schemas, source assets, generated assets, and final payloads.
- Require full preview before publication.
- Enforce minimum and maximum post counts.
- Reject duplicate images and malformed slide payloads.
- Bind a preview receipt to the exact content being published.
- Persist stable post IDs and fixed-window metric snapshots.

Deliverable: traces that explain each run.

### Phase 2: Split the monolith and build replay

- Extract provider and tool adapters behind typed interfaces.
- Add mock implementations and frozen fixtures.
- Build deterministic checks and regression cases.
- Add fault injection for each external dependency.
- Preserve the original single-file behavior as a compatibility baseline.

Deliverable: local tests that require no publication.

### Phase 3: Introduce Codex as a reviewed engineering agent

- Add `AGENTS.md`, task templates, output schemas, and protected-path rules.
- Run Codex in isolated worktrees with workspace-scoped permissions.
- Start with Plan, Review, Debug, and Implement modes.
- Require a human to approve every patch and experiment manifest.
- Store Codex transcripts, diffs, test results, and review decisions.

Deliverable: reviewed engineering patches.

### Phase 4: Add controlled draft canaries

- Allow a passing candidate to create a draft on a designated test account.
- Run visual, provenance, claim, and disclosure checks on the final artifact.
- Require human approval to publish.
- Collect fixed-window outcomes through the locked evaluator.
- Compare treatment against a concurrent blocked baseline.

Deliverable: a controlled online trial with a rollback point.

### Phase 5: Automate promotion within narrow boundaries

Automate low-risk promotion only after offline and online gates demonstrate reliability.

Early candidates could include:

- parser fixes;
- retry and timeout handling;
- trace completeness;
- renderer validation;
- budget enforcement;
- memory retrieval changes that pass replay;
- switching among already-approved prompt variants.

Keep these changes under review:

- publishing permissions;
- content-policy logic;
- provenance thresholds;
- health-claim policy;
- primary metrics;
- promotion rules;
- production credentials;
- changes that expand Codex’s editable scope.

Expand autonomy only where reliability has been demonstrated.

## The experiments I would run first

With traces and replay in place, I would test:

### Does a separate visual critic improve the final artifact?

A separate critic may catch repeated images, inconsistent people, overflow, or artificial compositions. It may also increase cost and over-edit good work.

Test visible defects offline before publication.

### Does structured memory outperform free-form notes?

Replace or supplement the ten notes with evidence-linked beliefs, account-specific hypotheses, and expiry dates.

Replay would test relevant memory use and rejection of stale or contradicted beliefs. Live trials would test account-adjusted performance consistency.

### Is candidate generation better than single-path creation?

Instead of committing to one strategy, generate several cheap concepts, score them against current evidence, and spend image-generation budget on the strongest.

A critic may favor consensus and reject unusual, promising ideas. Measure diversity, cost, and live outcomes.

### How much research is enough?

Six Lightreel calls is a budget, not a proven optimum. Compare four, six, and eight calls on source breadth, decisions, cost, and views.

Query diversity, full-post inspection, or a separate review of copy against evidence may matter more than call count.

### Should planning and execution use different models?

One model could choose the thesis and sources; another could create and inspect the post. Specialization may help, but handoffs may lose information.

Compare system outcomes and trace quality across these configurations.

### Does source similarity predict either performance or risk?

Source lineage would let us test the prompt’s assumption that close adaptation improves views. Compare originality bands on views, reviewer concern, and platform outcomes.

This could locate where learning a format stops helping and duplication risk begins.

## What this becomes beyond TikTok

A TikTok carousel is the first environment. The proposed engineering loop could serve other marketing systems:

- SEO and AEO recommendations generated from public-web evidence;
- paid-media agents that propose and test campaign changes;
- sales-content agents that build materials from product and customer evidence;
- brand-monitoring agents that investigate emerging narratives;
- content operations that generate, review, publish, and learn across channels.

Each would need to:

1. observe an environment;
2. preserve the evidence;
3. make a bounded decision;
4. act through controlled tools;
5. capture the trace and artifact;
6. measure the external result;
7. turn recurring failures into evals;
8. give Codex a narrow engineering task;
9. validate before promotion.

This connects to Atlas: models propose interpretations and actions, while raw observations remain inspectable. Derived claims must cite those observations, and independent evaluation must precede execution.

## The durable asset is the learning system

A successful post may fade with its trend. An explanation of improvement can inform the next experiment.

The retained work accumulates: traces, replay environments, regressions, source graphs, task contracts, results, and release controls.

ViralBench demonstrates a live multimodal marketing loop. The next question is whether we can improve it systematically while distinguishing progress from randomness and learning from imitation.

ViralBench supplies the environment; Codex would propose engineering changes. The proposed harness would test whether those changes improve the agent.

---

## Frequently asked questions

### What is ViralBench?

ViralBench gives frontier models TikTok accounts and tools to research posts, inspect media, generate images, preview carousels, and publish. They pursue views in the fitness category.

### What is an AI agent harness?

A harness surrounds a model with instructions, tools, schemas, memory, permissions, an execution loop, tests, traces, validation, and deployment controls. Different context and feedback can change the same model’s performance.

### How would Codex use ViralBench as a harness?

Codex would inspect failures and evaluation reports, edit a defined repository surface, run replay and regressions, and submit a patch for review. ViralBench would supply the environment and live outcomes.

### Is ViralBench measuring the model or the whole system?

The result reflects the model, prompt, research, image generator, tools, account, timing, memory, and platform. Compare configured systems; the experiment cannot isolate intelligence.

### Can an AI agent safely improve another AI agent?

Bounded work and independent evaluation could make this viable. Separate the builder from raw-evidence control, success metrics, evaluation, publishing credentials, and release approval. Use sandboxes, protected paths, locked evaluations, review, and rollback.

### Why not optimize only for views?

An unconstrained views objective may reward copying, sensational claims, and short-term tactics. Platform, provenance, factuality, cost, and publishing checks should pass before outcome optimization.

### Why is offline replay necessary if TikTok is the real evaluator?

Replay catches research gaps, broken tools, incomplete previews, duplicate assets, stale memory, and policy violations cheaply and repeatedly. It cannot predict TikTok distribution. Passing replay qualifies a candidate for live testing.
